sections.h2: Who values and bills a house in Paterson, NJ?
sections.html:
In Paterson the Tax Assessor's Office values every parcel, and the city's tax collector sends the bill. The assessor's page says its job covers appraising land and buildings under state statute, keeping ownership and transfer records current, checking building permits and maintaining values. The same office approves veteran, senior and disabled deductions and puts together the added and omitted assessment list.

The assessor's office is in City Hall, 155 Market Street, and keeps weekday counter hours that end at 4:30 p.m. Assessment appeals go to the Passaic County Board of Taxation in Totowa, and the assessor represents the city at those hearings and in New Jersey Tax Court. For a due date or a payoff amount on a specific parcel, ask the Paterson tax collector at City Hall for the figure in writing.

sections.h2: What does Paterson look like for a seller?
sections.html:
Paterson is the biggest city in Passaic County and a tightly packed one, with 161,793 residents in 2025 on 8.41 square miles of land, about 18,986 per square mile at the 2020 count. The Great Falls of the Passaic River, 77 feet high, powered the mills that earned it the name Silk City, and the Society for Establishing Useful Manufactures founded the town in 1791. The state chartered it as a city in 1851.

For 2020 to 2024 the survey shows a typical owned home at $360,100, typical rent at $1,548 and typical household income at $55,997. Only 26.9% of housing is owner-occupied, so many Paterson sellers are small landlords with two-, three- or four-family houses. Paterson counts 49,865 households of 3.15 people on average, and 44.6% of residents were born outside the country.

Paterson borders Clifton, Haledon, Hawthorne, Prospect Park, Totowa and Woodland Park in Passaic County and Elmwood Park and Fair Lawn in Bergen County. Interstate 80 runs through the city and the Garden State Parkway passes its southern edge. The city also contains the Great Falls historic district and the Eastside Park historic district. Children under 18 make up 27.7% of residents, and 67.3% of residents age 5 and over speak a language other than English at home, so listing materials in more than one language can reach more buyers.

sections.h2: Did Paterson revalue homes for 2026, and how do I appeal?
sections.html:
Yes. The Passaic County Board of Taxation names Paterson as the town that revalued or reassessed for 2026, which pushed the city's appeal cutoff to May 1 that year. That deadline has passed for 2026, but the same pattern applies after any later citywide revaluation.

  • A regular appeal reaches the county board by April 1, or 45 days after the notices were bulk mailed if that comes later.
  • Assessments above $1,000,000 can skip the board and be filed in state Tax Court.
  • Added and omitted assessments are appealed before December 1.
  • A board judgment can be carried to Tax Court inside 45 days.

The board's guidance says not to file until the assessment card has arrived, which is after February 1. After a revaluation, assessments are meant to equal market value as of the prior October 1, so recent Paterson sales before that date are the best evidence. Added or omitted assessment bills are generally sent in October and payable November 1.

sections.h2: Which deductions can lower a Paterson tax bill?
sections.html:
The assessor's page lists three local benefits, each applied for through the assessor with a claim form. The deductions reduce the bill for qualified owners, and the exemption removes it for a narrow group.

Paterson Tax Assessor deductions and exemptions, per the city's published eligibility notes
BenefitAmountMain eligibility testClaim form
Veteran or surviving spouse deduction$250 a yearOwner and New Jersey resident on October 1 of the pre-tax year; qualifying wartime or peacekeeping serviceV.S.S.
Senior, disabled or surviving spouse deduction$250 a yearAge 65 or older, or permanently disabled, as of December 31; income under $10,000 excluding certain benefitsPTD
Disabled veteran exemptionFull exemption of home and lotCertified 100% permanently and totally disabled by the VA; owner and residentD.V.S.S.E.

Veteran applicants need a copy of the DD-214, and the veteran and senior claim forms can be filed with either the assessor or the collector. The disabled veteran claim can be filed at any time of year. State programs such as ANCHOR and Senior Freeze are separate, and the 2025 application deadline of November 2, 2026 has passed.

sections.h2: How does Paterson's local economy bear on home values?
sections.html:
Paterson's workforce is large and local. The Census shows 63.6% of residents 16 and older in the civilian labor force, with a mean commute of 22.6 minutes, shorter than in Old Bridge or Ocean County. Hospitals and social services took in about $1.37 billion in 2022, and retail sales were about $1.56 billion, or $9,981 per resident, well under the Passaic County figure.

The poverty rate was 21.2% and the share of residents without health insurance under 65 was 21.3%, so many owners have limited room to absorb a surprise tax bill. An owner who misses a first quarter installment should call the collector early, since interest starts on the due date and each skipped quarter adds to the debt.

sections.h2: What happens if Paterson property tax goes unpaid?
sections.html:
Paterson sells unpaid tax liens at an online auction. The city's notice for the sale of 2023 delinquent taxes and municipal charges set the bidding for December 11, 2024 at 10:00 a.m. on the city's New Jersey tax sale site. Parcel lists, delinquency amounts and costs are free to view, and bidding follows the instructions posted on that site.

State law allows an accelerated sale when taxes or liens are still open on the 11th day of the eleventh month of the fiscal year. The city fixes its own late interest inside the state ceiling and may allow ten days of grace. A tax sale certificate is a recorded claim against the parcel, and a seller must redeem or cancel it before title is clear.

  • Request a payoff letter that covers the closing date.
  • Ask the Passaic County Clerk whether any tax sale certificate is on record.
  • Redeem the certificate before closing so title is clear.

sections.h2: What else should a Paterson seller check before listing?
sections.html:
Ask the city for open permits and violations before you list. After Hurricane Irene in August 2011 the Passaic River rose to levels unseen for a century, so buyers may ask about past water in basements. The Paterson School District covers all the area inside the city limits.

Recording happens at the Passaic County Clerk, whose published fee schedule also carries the realty transfer tax table by price band. Because the assessor keeps transfer records, the tax roll changes owners once the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Where is the Paterson Tax Assessor's Office?
faqs.a: City Hall, 155 Market Street, Paterson. The assessor's page gives weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

faqs.q: When was the Paterson appeal deadline for 2026?
faqs.a: May 1, 2026, because Paterson underwent a revaluation or reassessment that year. The deadline for a regular appeal in other towns is April 1, and that window for 2026 has closed.

faqs.q: How much is the Paterson veteran property tax deduction?
faqs.a: The deduction is $250 a year for a qualified veteran or surviving spouse who owns the home and was a New Jersey resident on the prior October 1. A veteran rated 100% permanently and totally disabled by the VA may qualify for a complete exemption instead.
Yes. The city sold 2023 delinquent taxes in an online auction on December 11, 2024. Parcel details are posted on the city's New Jersey tax sale page.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Paterson house that owes property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The closing agent settles the arrears from the seller's proceeds. First get a payoff letter from the Paterson tax collector, and clear any tax sale certificate before closing.
